about.title: West Sacramento Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: West Sacramento residents rely on a mix of local clinics and larger Sacramento-area hospital systems for care, and most of those visits go fine. But when a diagnosis is missed, a surgery goes wrong, or medication is mismanaged, the harm can be lasting. California's MICRA law puts real structure around these claims: a short window to act, a required pre-suit notice, and a legal standard that asks whether a qualified provider would have acted differently — not simply whether the outcome was bad. That's why these cases usually need a medical expert early on to even move forward. If you believe a provider in West Sacramento or nearby Yolo County facilities made an error that hurt you or a family member, LawProactive can connect you with an independent attorney, free of charge, to review what happened.

Failure to monitor or follow up on abnormal results

whyChoose.title: What to Know Before You Act

items.title: The Clock Starts Early
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from when you discover the harm, and never more than three years from the injury itself, to bring a claim. Waiting to sort things out on your own can quietly cost you that window.

items.title: A 90-Day Notice Comes First
items.desc: Before a malpractice lawsuit can be filed, California law requires a 90-day notice to the provider. An attorney familiar with this step can help make sure it's handled correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Is Usually Required
items.desc: Because a bad outcome alone doesn't prove malpractice, these claims almost always need a qualified medical expert to evaluate the care you received before a case can move forward.

items.question: I had a bad outcome after surgery in West Sacramento — does that mean it was malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law requires showing that a provider's care fell below what a reasonably careful medical professional would have done, not just that the result was disappointing or unexpected. An independent attorney can help you understand whether your situation may meet that standard.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim?
items.answer: Generally, you have one year from when you discover the injury, and no more than three years from the date it happened, whichever comes first. There are exceptions, so it's worth getting a timeline reviewed sooner rather than later.

items.question: Do I need to notify the doctor or hospital before suing?
items.answer: Yes. California requires a 90-day pre-suit notice to the provider before a malpractice lawsuit can be filed. This step has specific timing and content requirements, which is one reason people connect with an attorney early.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover?
items.answer: California caps non-economic damages in malpractice cases, though that cap adjusts upward each year under current law. Economic losses like medical bills and lost income are generally handled separately from that cap.
